THIS R.F.A. HAVING BEEN HEARD AND RESERVED FOR JUDGMENT ON 29/03/2023 COMING ON FOR PRONOUNCEMENT OF ORDERS THIS DAY, THE COURT DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
 JUDGMENT

The plaintiffs are impugning the judgment and decree dated 27.01.2014 passed in O.S.No.3113/1993 on the file of the learned III Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge, B'lore City (CCH-25),
(hereinafter referred to as 'the Trial Court' for brevity), dismissing their suit filed for declaration and for permanent injunction and also to set aside the order passed in the eviction proceedings in HRC Nos.1255/1993, 359/1995, 2771/1993, 358/1995 and 696/1994 as the same is null and void and not binding on the plaintiffs.
2.

Brief facts of the case are that, plaintiff Nos.1 to 3 have filed the suit O.S.No.3113/1993 against defendant Nos.1 to 7 seeking the relief of declaration that the Will dated 21.02.1991 alleged to have been executed by late Malleshaiah and the General Power of Attorney stated to have been executed by the said Malleshaiah in favour of defendant No.2 as null and void and does not convey any right,
title or interest over the properties mentioned therein and consequently, to grant permanent injunction restraining the defendants from making use of the said Will and the GPA in any manner affecting the rights of the plaintiffs and for costs.

Subsequently, the plaint was amended by impleading defendant Nos.8 to 11, claiming declaration that the orders obtained by defendant Nos.1 to 3 and 7 in HRC Nos.128/1994, 1146/1993, 1319/1993 and 2712/1993 on the file of the Small Causes Court, Bangalore, against non-existent tenants in respect of the portions of the Suit Schedule Property are non-est, inoperative and the same is not binding on the plaintiffs and for further declaration that the eviction proceedings in HRC Nos.1255/1993, 359/1995, 2711/1993, 358/1995 and 696/1994 are null and void and these orders are not binding on the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs have also sought to set aside the Will dated 21.02.1991 as the same is null and void.

4. The Schedule appended to the plaint describes the land measuring 7  guntas in Sy.No.34 of Govinayakanahalli, Uttarahalli Hobli, Bangalore South Taluk, consisting of a building and vacant portion with the boundaries mentioned therein.
It is contended by the plaintiffs that plaintiff No.1- Govindamma is the second wife of Malleshaiah and plaintiff No.3 is the Son of plaintiff No.1 and Malleshaiah.
Plaintiff No.2 is also the Son of Malleshaiah through his first wife- Muniyamma.
Defendant No.2- Papamma is the daughter of plaintiff No.1 and Malleshaiah.
Defendant No.1 is the daughter of defendant No.2.
Defendant No.3 is the son of defendant No.1 and defendant No.4 is his wife.
Defendant Nos.5 and 6 are the children of defendant Nos.3 and 4.
Defendant No.7 is the Son of Papamma.
Papamma was married to one Eerasandrappa over 35 years ago and they have begotten defendant Nos.1, 3 and 7.

Late Malleshaiah and his brothers were having ancestral properties,
situated at Dombarapalya, Narasandra Dakhle, Kadur Hobli, Magadi Taluk.

The said Malleshaiah and his brothers negotiated for selling their ancestral properties for the purpose of purchasing the Sri Y M Muniswamy Alias M Raju vs Smt E Yellamma on 21 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/108035107/

5. It is contended that in the land bearing Sy.No.34 of Govinayakanahalli which was measuring 4.33 acres, late Malleshiah had put up construction during his lifetime and was living there with his family.
The property was enjoyed as Joint Family Property.
The land in Sy.Nos.35 and 36 were acquired by the Bangalore Development Authority ('BDA' for short) and Malleshaiah received compensation.
Out of Sy.No.34, the portion measuring 1.9 acres was given to Yellamma- sister of Malleshaiah.
The BDA initiated proceedings for acquiring Sy.No.34 as well.
However, 10 guntas of land was left from acquisition and the same was retained by Malleshaiah and 2 guntas of land which was also left from acquisition was retained by Yellamma.
Since there were buildings existing in the said 10 guntas of land, the same was not acquired by BDA, but left for enjoyment of Malleshaiah and his family.
There were 8 tenaments and 3 shops existing in the said 10 guntas of land.
There were 5 coconut trees and one old open well and other trees and plants.
Malleshaiah along with his family members was living in the portion of the said building, while the remaining portion was leased out.
The portion was in occupation of Papamma- defendant No.2 as she was allowed to live there with permission.
Except plaintiffs and defendant No.2, no one else were having any right, title or interest over this portion of the property.
It is contended that Malleshaiah died on 22.08.1991 at the age of 90 years in the house of the plaintiffs, leaving behind the plaintiffs and defendant No.2 to succeed to his estate.
He was not keeping good health two years prior to his death.
As he was suffering from various old age ailments, he was not having any idea to execute any Will in respect of the Joint Family Property.
He never executed any Will or other documents during his lifetime in respect of the Joint Family Property.
Moreover, he was not the absolute owner of the property.
After the death of Malleshaiah, the property was being enjoyed by the members of his family.

6. The plaintiffs contended that they came to know that the defendants E.Muniyappa, E.Muniraju and E. Yellamma filed the suit O.S.No.7619/1992 against plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 before the learned City Civil Judge, Bangalore seeking permanent injunction with regard to the Schedule Property i.e.,
site bearing Nos.2114 and 2115 stated to have been carved out of Sy.No.34 of Govinayakanahalli.
They contended that Malleshaiah had executed the Will dated 21.02.1991 bequeathing his properties in their favour.
They also contended that they are in possession of the same.
Defendant No.2 filed the suit O.S.No.903/1993 against the plaintiffs before the City Civil Court (CCH-16), Bangalore seeking partition and separate possession of her 1/4th share.
She contended that Malleshaiah had executed GPA in her favour giving her authority over Site No.2413 of Govinayakanahalli.
Defendant Nos.2, 3 and 7 managed to get ex-parte interim order in the said suit against the plaintiffs in respect of the Suit Schedule Property.
The defendants have deliberately suppressed the details of the Will and the Power of Attorney said to have been executed by late Malleshaiah.
Malleshaiah was not in a position to execute any document, due to his health condition.
Moreover, he had no authority to execute the documents.
It is alleged that defendant Nos.5 and 6 who are the grand children of Papamma and the children of K.Muniraju said to have acquired title under the Will over Sy.No.34 of Govinayakanahalli.
Therefore, all the defendants are impleaded in the suit.

13. On the basis of these pleadings, the Trial Court framed the following issues;
1) Whether the plaintiffs prove that the suit schedule property is a joint family property and one deceased Malleshaiah and plaintiff No.1 and defendant No.1 are entitle for 1/15th share each in the suit schedule property out of the share of the deceased Malleshaiah?
2) Whether defendants prove that the suit schedule property was the self acquired property of Malleshaiah and the same was bequeathed under a Will dtd.21.2.91 in favour of the 2nd defendant?
3) Whether the plaintiffs prove that the Will dtd.21.2.91 in favour of 2nd defendant and Power of Attorney of the same date in favour of 2nd defendant are null and void and non-est in law?
4) Whether the plaintiffs further prove that they are in possession of some portion of the suit schedule property?

6) Whether the defendants prove that they are in possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule property?
7) Whether the defendants prove the suit schedule property is not properly described and the same is properly described and the same is properly described in the written statement?
8)
Whether the suit is not maintainable in view of the pendency of O.S.No.905/93?
9) Whether there is any cause action for the suit?
10) Whether plaintiffs are entitled for suit remedies?

15. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree passed by the trial Court,
the plaintiffs are before this Court.
16. Heard Sri K.S.Ramesh & Sri R.Vijayakumar, learned counsel for the appellants/plaintiffs and Sri G.Shankar, learned counsel for respondent Nos.1 to 4, 6 and 7.
Perused the materials including the trial Court records.
17. Learned counsel for the appellants contended that the defendants have not proved the execution of the Will dated 21.02.1991.
The testator- Malleshaiah died on 22.08.1991 at the age of 90 years.
There is no explanation as to why Malleshaiah excluded his second wife and her son Raju and also his Son- Papaiah.
The Will in question is not proved in accordance with law.
None of the attesting witnesses were examined.
Even though the defendants examined defendant No.7 as DW- 1, he was not present when the Will in question was said to have been executed and DW-2 is not the attesting witness.
Apart from these witnesses, the defendants have not examined any other witnesses.
Under such circumstances, the Will in question is not proved.
There is always a presumption in favour of jointness amongst the members of the family.
The left hand thumb impression on Ex.D45 is not admitted.
When the plaintiffs have not admitted the left hand thumb impression of Malleshaiah, but disputed the same.
But the defendants have not sought to be sent the disputed document for scientific examination.
The register maintained by the Sub-registrar containing the left hand thumb impression of Malleshaiah was also not summoned.
Under such circumstances, it cannot be held that the Will in question is not proved by the plaintiffs.

18. Learned counsel has placed reliance on the decisions of the Hon'ble Apex Court in (1) Shivakumar & Ors. Vs.Sharanabasappa & Ors.1 (2) S.R.Srinivasa & Ors. Vs.
S.Padmavathamma2 and (3) Sri J.T. Surappa & Anr. Vs. Sri Satchidhanandendra Saraswathi Swamiji Public Charitable Trust and Others3 in support of his contention that the Will is not proved in accordance with law.

The conduct of the plaintiffs discloses that they are bent upon to tease and harass the defendants without description of the properties and without disclosing the pendency of the suit and alienating the sites.

Even though,
there is no stay for the final decree proceedings in OS.No.905/1993, the same is being dragged on without any valid reasons.

There is no reason to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court.

24. In view of the rival contentions taken by the parties to lis, the point that would arise for my consideration is;
"Whether the impugned judgment and decree passed by the trial Court calls for interference by this Court?
What order?"

My answer to the above point is in the 'Negative' for the following;
REASONS 25.
The relationship between the parties are not in dispute.
It is specific contention of the plaintiffs that schedule properties are the joint family properties of Malleshaiah.
Similarly, contention by the plaintiffs and other family members in OS.No.905/1993 was negatived by the trial Court.

The defendant herein produced Ex.D3- the grant certificate dated 30.06.1966 issued by the Tashildar,
Bangalore South Taluk in favour of Malleshaiah.
The subject matter of the grant certificate includes Sy.No.34 measuring 4.36 acres.
The grant certificate refers Malleshaiah seeking occupancy right, as he purchased it from the inamdar.
From this document, it cannot be made out that it was a joint family property of Malleshaiah and his brothers.
Even though the plaintiffs have contended that it is the joint family property, but they have not produced any document in support of the same.
Under such circumstances.
I am of the opinion that the contention of the plaintiffs in that regard is to be rejected.
26. One of the grounds raised by the plaintiffs to deny the execution of the registered Will by Malleshaiah is that he had no authority to bequeath the property since it was a joint family property.
In view of the discussions held above, such stand taken by the plaintiffs are liable to be rejected.
27. The original Will dated 21.02.1991 is produced by the defendants as per Ex.D45.
It is pertinent to note that the Will dated 21.2.1991 is a registered document.
The testator describes himself as aged 74 years residing in the house constructed on site Nos.2414, 2415, 2434 and 2433.
The testator further states that after the death of his first wife he married Smt. Govindamma, who is the sister of his first wife.
He refers to his son Muniswamy alias Raju, who is none other than plaintiff No.2 and states that he is already married and he is residing at Kuppam on his avocation.
He refers defendant No.2- Papamma and her children stating that the husband of Papamma was addicted to bad vices and has deserted his wife and children.
Therefore, Papamma- defendant No.2 along with her children was residing with Malleshaiah and during his old age, they were looking after him.

Sy.No.34 of Govinayahalli was self acquired property consisting of sites over 10 cents of land, which Sri Y M Muniswamy Alias M Raju vs Smt E Yellamma on 21 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/108035107/

2. 3. Unlike other documents, the will speaks from the death of the testator and therefore the maker of the will is never available for deposing as to the circumstances in which the will came to be executed.
This aspect introduces an element of solemnity in the decision of the question whether the document propounded is proved to be the last will and testament of the testator.
Normally, the onus which lies on the propounder can be taken to be discharged on proof of the essential facts which go into the making of the will.

A shaky signature, a feeble mind, an unfair and unjust disposition of property, the propounder himself taking a leading part in the making of the will under which he receives a substantial benefit and such other circumstances raise suspicious about the execution of the will.

Finally, it is the test of satisfaction of the judicial conscious, which is to be applied while considering the Will.
Since, the Will unlike any other adjacent speaks after the death of the testator, the duty cast on the Courts to consider the recitals in the Will by applying the armchair rule i.e., the court puts itself in the position of the testator to consider the will from his view point in the light of the surrounding facts and circumstances.
Every other possibility cannot be held as suspicious circumstances.
In the present case, the reference to the Will and its recitals disclose that the testator has given sufficient explanation for bequeathing two sites in favour of his grand children and to exclude his other legal heirs.
